blocks.content: Your car has a check engine light. It's great at telling you about problems the manufacturer already thought of: low oil pressure, overheating engine, a loose gas cap. One light, a handful of known failure modes, and a warning on the dashboard the moment one of them trips.

Now imagine your engine starts making a weird noise nobody predicted. The check engine light stays off, because nobody wired up a sensor for a weird noise. A good mechanic handles this differently. They plug in a diagnostic scanner, pull raw sensor data straight off the engine, and start asking questions nobody thought to ask in advance. That difference, dashboard versus raw signal, is basically the whole difference between monitoring and observability.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396347430-28336261.png
blocks.alt: Known dashboard questions on one side, raw signal answering unknown questions on the other

blocks.content: Monitoring is the dashboard. It tells you when something you already predicted goes wrong. Observability is the raw signal underneath everything, rich enough that you can ask a question you never anticipated and still get an answer, without shipping new code first.
Observability is the ability to ask new questions about your system without shipping new code to answer them.
1. Introduction

Every production system eventually breaks in a way nobody built a dashboard for. Maybe it's a slow query that only shows up for users in one region, or a memory leak that only triggers after exactly six hours of uptime. Monitoring can't catch what it wasn't built to catch.

Monitoring works off dashboards and alerts you set up ahead of time, for failure modes you already know about: CPU too high, disk almost full, error rate above 1 percent. It's essential, but it only answers questions someone thought to ask months ago.

Observability flips that around. Instead of pre building an answer for every possible question, you collect enough raw, high quality signal, logs, metrics, and traces, that you can slice it after the fact for a question you're only now discovering you need to ask.

{"headers":["Monitoring","Observability"],"rows":[["Answers questions you already anticipated","Lets you ask new questions on the fly"],["Built around dashboards and static thresholds","Built around rich, raw, queryable signal"],["Good for known failure modes","Good for unknown failure modes"],["Tells you something is wrong","Tells you why it's wrong"]]}

blocks.title: Not a replacement
blocks.content: Monitoring isn't obsolete. You still want alert thresholds for the failures you already know about. Observability is what saves you the day something new breaks.
2. The three pillars
Observability isn't one tool, it's three different kinds of signal working together: logs, metrics, and traces. Each one is good at a different job, and none of them alone gives you the full picture.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396347432-374663434.png
blocks.alt: One request producing three separate signals: logs, metrics, and traces

blocks.content: 2.1 Logs
A log is a single, timestamped event. "User 4521 hit checkout at 10:32:01 and got a 500 error" is a log line. It's a fact about one specific moment, with as much detail as you decide to record.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396347432-934448208.png
blocks.alt: A single timestamped log line carrying detail about one error

blocks.content: Logs are best when you already know roughly where to look and you need the full detail: the exact error message, the stack trace, the request body, every field that led up to the failure. They answer "what exactly happened here."

{
  "timestamp": "2026-07-08T10:32:01.442Z",
  "level": "error",
  "service": "checkout",
  "userId": "4521",
  "traceId": "8f14e45f2b3c",
  "message": "checkout request failed",
  "statusCode": 500
}

blocks.title: Structure matters
blocks.content: Plain text lines like console.log('something broke') are hard to search once you have millions of them. Structured logs, JSON with consistent field names, are what actually make logs queryable at scale.
2.2 Metrics

A metric is a number, measured over time. Requests per second, average latency, error rate, memory usage. Instead of storing every single event, you aggregate it: a count, a sum, a percentile, bucketed into small time windows.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396347433-55571645.png
blocks.alt: Individual requests rolled up into one aggregated metric value

blocks.content: Metrics are cheap to store and fast to query, even across months of history, because you're storing aggregates instead of raw events. That's exactly why they're the backbone of dashboards and alerting thresholds: page someone if error rate crosses 5 percent for 2 minutes.

{"headers":["Metric type","What it tracks"],"rows":[["Counter","A value that only goes up, like total requests served"],["Gauge","A value that goes up and down, like current memory usage"],["Histogram","A distribution of values, like the spread of request latencies"]]}

blocks.title: Low granularity by design
blocks.content: A metric can tell you error rate jumped from 1 percent to 40 percent. It can't tell you which specific request failed or why. That detail is gone the moment you aggregate.
2.3 Traces

A trace follows one single request as it travels through your system: the API gateway, an internal service, a database call, another service, all the way back to the response. Each hop is recorded as a span, with its own start time and duration.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396347433-36638964.png
blocks.alt: One request traced across a gateway, an inventory service, and a payment service

blocks.content: Traces are best for distributed systems, where a single user action fans out into a handful of internal calls. When something is slow or broken, a trace tells you exactly which hop in that chain is the problem, not just that the overall request was slow.

blocks.title: Instrumentation has to be complete
blocks.content: Tracing only works if every service in the call path is instrumented and forwards the trace context onward. Skip one hop and you get a gap, a black box where you can't see what happened.
3. Why you need all three together
blocks.text: 3. Why you need all three together

blocks.content: None of the three pillars alone tells the whole story. They're complementary, and a real incident usually walks through all three in order.
A metric tells you the error rate spiked at 10:32. That is your signal that something is wrong, but it does not say what.
A trace, pulled from that same time window, shows you that the payment service specifically is taking 8 seconds instead of 80 milliseconds. Now you know where.
A log, pulled using that trace ID, shows you the exact exception: a connection pool exhausted error with a full stack trace. Now you know why.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396347434-448155339.png
blocks.alt: An error rate metric crossing its alert threshold

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pillar","Best for","Granularity"],"rows":[["Logs","Deep detail on one event","Very high, one event at a time"],["Metrics","Trends and alerting","Low, aggregated over time"],["Traces","Where time went across services","Medium, one request end to end"]]}

blocks.title: Cost adds up fast
blocks.content: Logs and traces are far more expensive to store than metrics, because you are keeping raw data instead of aggregates. Most teams sample traces, keeping every trace above a latency threshold plus a small random slice of the rest, and set shorter retention windows on logs to keep storage cost sane.
Metrics tell you something is wrong. Traces tell you where. Logs tell you why.
4. The correlation problem
Knowing you need all three pillars is easy. Actually jumping between them during an incident, fast, while things are on fire, is the hard part. This is usually called the correlation problem.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396347435-892496183.png
blocks.alt: Pivoting from an alert's time window into the traces that happened during it

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396347435-403010966.png
blocks.alt: Pivoting from one slow trace span into its matching log line

blocks.content: The trick that makes this practical is a single ID threaded through everything, usually called a trace ID or a request ID. It gets generated once, at the very first hop of a request, and every service downstream carries it forward: on every span, on every log line, on every metric label where it makes sense.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396347436-641074143.png
blocks.alt: Logs, metrics, and traces all linked back to one shared trace ID

blocks.content: With that ID in place, an engineer can go from a metric spike at 10:32, to the traces between 10:30 and 10:34, to the slowest one, to every log line carrying that exact trace ID. Three pillars, one thread connecting them.

blocks.title: Timestamps alone are not enough
blocks.content: Without a shared ID you are stuck correlating by timestamp, and clock drift between services can be off by seconds. That is more than enough to point you at the wrong request entirely.
5. Tooling that unifies the three pillars
blocks.text: 5. Tooling that unifies the three pillars

blocks.content: You don't have to hand build this. A handful of tools exist specifically to store all three pillars and let you pivot between them from one screen.

["Grafana plus Prometheus, Loki, and Tempo: metrics in Prometheus, logs in Loki, traces in Tempo, all viewed in one Grafana dashboard with click through links between them.","Datadog: a single hosted platform covering logs, metrics, and traces (APM), with correlation built in by default.","New Relic: similar full stack coverage, strong on automatic instrumentation for popular frameworks.","OpenTelemetry: not a backend at all, but the vendor neutral standard for instrumenting your code once and shipping logs, metrics, and traces to whichever backend you choose."]
items: Grafana plus Prometheus, Loki, and Tempo: metrics in Prometheus, logs in Loki, traces in Tempo, all viewed in one Grafana dashboard with click through links between them.
Datadog: a single hosted platform covering logs, metrics, and traces (APM), with correlation built in by default.
New Relic: similar full stack coverage, strong on automatic instrumentation for popular frameworks.
OpenTelemetry: not a backend at all, but the vendor neutral standard for instrumenting your code once and shipping logs, metrics, and traces to whichever backend you choose.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396347437-647711563.png
blocks.alt: An instrumented app sending logs, metrics, and traces through OpenTelemetry to separate backends

blocks.content: OpenTelemetry matters because it decouples instrumentation from the backend. You add the SDK to your code once, and you can swap Datadog for Grafana later without re instrumenting every service.

blocks.title: Pick the standard before the vendor
blocks.content: Using a different tool per pillar without a shared trace ID standard defeats the whole point. Standardize how IDs propagate before you pick vendors, not after.
6. Worked example: an incident from alert to root cause
blocks.text: 6. Worked example: an incident from alert to root cause

blocks.title: Scenario: checkout is failing intermittently
blocks.text: Your online store's checkout flow calls three internal services: the API gateway, an inventory service, and a payment service. Users start reporting failed checkouts around 10:30 AM.

blocks.content: Step one. A metric alert fires: checkout error rate crossed 5 percent, triggered by the alerting rule watching the gateway's error counter. An engineer gets paged.

Step two. The engineer opens the tracing UI, filters to failed checkout traces between 10:28 and 10:34, and picks one. The trace shows the request spent 40 milliseconds in the gateway, 30 milliseconds in inventory, then 9 seconds stuck in the payment service before failing.

Step three. The engineer copies that trace's ID and searches the log system for it. One log line comes back: a connection pool exhausted exception, thrown right as the payment service tried to open a new database connection.

Root cause: a recent deploy dropped the payment service connection pool size from 50 to 5. Under normal load that is fine. Under the morning traffic spike, every connection was checked out and new requests queued until they timed out.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396348090-254156977.png
blocks.alt: Incident flow moving from alert to trace to log to root cause

blocks.content: Total time from page to root cause: about six minutes. Without traces, the engineer would have been guessing which of three services was slow. Without a shared trace ID, finding the one relevant log line out of millions would have taken far longer than six minutes.
7. Implementation: propagating a trace ID

Let's make the correlation ID idea concrete. The core pattern is simple: generate an ID at the first hop, read it back out at every hop after that, and attach it to every span, log line, and outgoing request.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396348092-434154933.png
blocks.alt: A trace ID generated at the gateway and carried through two downstream services

blocks.content: Here is a small Express middleware that either picks up an incoming trace ID header or generates a new one, then makes it available to the rest of the request:
Now, when this service calls a downstream service, it forwards that same ID as a header:
And every log line the service writes includes that same ID as a field, not just a message string:

blocks.title: The weak link is easy to miss
blocks.content: It is easy to forget to propagate the trace ID on retries, background jobs, or queue consumers picking up a message later. Any hop that drops the ID breaks the chain, and you are back to guessing which log lines belong to which request.
8. The interview angle

In a system design interview, observability is easy to skip because it doesn't feel like part of the architecture. Treating it as an afterthought is a mistake, and interviewers notice when a candidate brings it up on their own.

You don't need to draw all three pillars in detail. What matters is showing you know they exist, they serve different purposes, and you would design for correlation from day one, not bolt it on after the first bad incident.

["Mention logs, metrics, and traces by name, and say what each one is for.","Say you would generate a trace ID at the edge, the API gateway or load balancer, and propagate it through every service.","Name a real tool or standard, Prometheus and Grafana, Datadog, or OpenTelemetry, so it does not sound theoretical.","Tie it back to the actual system: what would you alert on, and what would you want to be able to ask later that you cannot predict now?"]
items: Mention logs, metrics, and traces by name, and say what each one is for.
Say you would generate a trace ID at the edge, the API gateway or load balancer, and propagate it through every service.
Name a real tool or standard, Prometheus and Grafana, Datadog, or OpenTelemetry, so it does not sound theoretical.
Tie it back to the actual system: what would you alert on, and what would you want to be able to ask later that you cannot predict now?

blocks.content: Good HLD candidates don't just design for the happy path, they design for the moment things break and someone has ten minutes to find out why.
